name: Estradiol
route_note: oral tablets; transdermal patches, gels and sprays; vaginal tablets, rings and creams; IM valerate or cypionate depot

discovery.by: Edward Doisy and colleagues (Saint Louis University)
discovery.note: Isolated from sow ovaries in 1935; estrone had been isolated by Doisy and Butenandt in 1929.

tagline: The main human estrogen, used in menopausal hormone therapy and gender-affirming care
summary: Estradiol is the most potent naturally occurring human estrogen. It is used to relieve menopausal symptoms, prevent postmenopausal osteoporosis, treat hypoestrogenism and as part of feminising hormone therapy; women with a uterus also need a progestogen to protect the endometrium.
mechanism: Estradiol binds nuclear estrogen receptors α and β, which dimerise and regulate gene transcription through estrogen-response elements and interactions with other transcription factors. It also signals rapidly via membrane receptors including GPER.

In menopause, replacing estradiol stabilises hypothalamic thermoregulation (reducing hot flushes), maintains vaginal and urogenital epithelium, and reduces bone resorption. Unopposed estrogen stimulates endometrial proliferation, so a progestogen is added in women with a uterus.
uses: Hypoestrogenism due to hypogonadism, castration or primary ovarian insufficiency
Feminising gender-affirming hormone therapy (off-label in many labels)
Palliation of advanced prostate and breast cancer (selected cases)

history.title: Estrone isolated
history.detail: Doisy and Butenandt independently isolate estrone from urine.

history.title: Estradiol isolated
history.detail: Doisy's group isolates estradiol from ovarian tissue.

history.title: Endometrial cancer link
history.detail: Studies link unopposed estrogen therapy to endometrial cancer, leading to combined estrogen–progestogen regimens.

history.title: Transdermal patch
history.detail: Twice-weekly estradiol matrix patches widen transdermal use, which avoids first-pass liver effects.

history.title: Women's Health Initiative
history.detail: WHI reports increased breast cancer, stroke and VTE with oral conjugated estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone, prompting class boxed warnings.

history.title: Boxed warnings to be removed
history.detail: In November 2025 FDA announces it will ask manufacturers to remove boxed warnings on menopausal hormone therapy.

pk.half_life: about 13–20 h (oral, including recycling via estrone)
pk.bioavailability: about 5% oral (micronised); transdermal avoids first pass
pk.metabolism: hepatic conversion to estrone and estriol; CYP3A4, CYP1A2; sulfation and glucuronidation

serious: endometrial hyperplasia and cancer if unopposed
breast cancer with combined long-term therapy
safety.boxed_warning: Class warning (US): endometrial cancer, cardiovascular disorders, breast cancer and probable dementia, based on WHI; in November 2025 FDA announced these boxed warnings would be removed from menopausal hormone therapy labels.

facts: Transdermal estradiol carries a lower risk of venous thromboembolism than oral estrogen in observational studies.
The WHI trials tested conjugated equine estrogens, not estradiol, but their findings were applied across the estrogen class.
